facts.statement: Imperobator lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian)

facts.statement: Imperobator inhabited what is now James Ross Island in Antarctica during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now James Ross Island in Antarctica

facts.statement: The only originally described specimen of Imperobator was discovered in 2003 by an expedition from the University of California Museum of Paleontology.
facts.quote: The only described specimen was found in 2003 by an expedition launched by the University of California Museum of Paleontology

facts.statement: The fossil was initially classified as a dromaeosaur in 2007.
facts.quote: initially described as a dromaeosaur in 2007

facts.statement: Fossils of Imperobator were unearthed in December 2003.
facts.quote: Fossils of a large theropod dinosaur were unearthed in December 2003

facts.statement: The fossils were found on the Naze Peninsula of James Ross Island, Antarctica, by an expedition mounted by the University of California Museum of Paleontology.
facts.quote: by a fossil hunting expedition that had been mounted by the University of California Museum of Paleontology to the Naze Peninsula of James Ross Island, Antarctica

facts.statement: The fossils belong to the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation, dating to approximately 71 million years ago in the early Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: These belong to the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation, which dates to the early Maastrictian age of the Late Cretaceous (~71 mya)

facts.statement: Ricardo Ely and Judd Case formally described Imperobator antarcticus as a new genus and species in 2019.
facts.quote: The specimen was formally described as the holotype of a new genus and species, Imperobator antarcticus, by American paleontologists Ricardo Ely and Judd Case in 2019

facts.statement: The genus name Imperobator means "powerful warrior" in Latin.
facts.quote: The generic name derives from the Latin for "powerful warrior"

facts.statement: The species name antarcticus refers to the continent of Antarctica where the specimen was found.
facts.quote: The specific name refers to the continent in which the specimen was discovered

facts.statement: Imperobator is one of only two non-avian theropod dinosaurs known from Antarctica.
facts.quote: Imperobator is one of only two non-avian theropods known from Antarctica

facts.statement: Imperobator crossed to Antarctica when the continent was still part of the supercontinent Gondwana.
facts.quote: crossing over to the landmass when it was part of Gondwana

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of an incomplete isolated left foot including part of the shin bone, ankle bones, and toe claws, along with teeth and skull fragments.
facts.quote: The only described specimen was found in 2003 by an expedition launched by the University of California Museum of Paleontology and initially described as a dromaeosaur in 2007

facts.statement: The original specimen includes an incomplete left foot with parts of the tibia, ankle bones, and claws, as well as teeth and other bone fragments.
facts.quote: consisting mostly of an incomplete isolated left pes including a portion of the tibia, an incomplete astragalus, a partial calcaneus and fibula, ungual, partial phalanges and metacarpals, though teeth are known as well

facts.statement: Additional fossils associated with the original specimen include skull fragments, a tail vertebra, more teeth, and foot elements held by other institutions.
facts.quote: additional fossils were located in the facilities of Eastern Washington University and the South Dakota School of Mines and Technology that pertain to UCMP 276000 including skull fragments which may be from the premaxilla, maxilla, and/or dentary as well as a caudal vertebra, more teeth, and pedal elements

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Imperobator measures approximately 45 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen measures approximately 45 cm in length

facts.statement: Reexaminations of specific bones revised the estimated body length of Imperobator to between 2 and 3 meters.
facts.quote: reexaminations of the phalanx III-1 and distal metatarsal III of Imperobator suggested that they were much smaller than those of Austroraptor and more similar in size to those of Neuquenraptor and Deinonychus, which led to the revision of its body length estimate to around 2 - 3 m

facts.statement: Imperobator is classified within the clade Paraves rather than Dromaeosauridae due to traits such as the absence of a sickle claw and a smooth distal metatarsal II.
facts.quote: Despite prior assignment to Dromaeosauridae, Imperobator has since been assigned to the clade Paraves due to certain characteristics that differ from those of dromaeosaurids, including the lack of a sickle claw, the smooth surface of the distal metatarsal II and the lack of an ungual on the second pedal digit

facts.statement: Preserved skull fragments contain long, curved, and bladed teeth similar to those of other carnivorous paravian dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Undescribed cranial material preserves teeth from the maxilla and dentary, which were long, curved, and bladed like in other carnivorous paravians

facts.statement: Imperobator possesses a unique trait where the ankle bones (calcanea) are fused with the fibulae.
facts.quote: both calcanea are preserved and are fused with the fibulae, a unique trait of the genus

facts.statement: Metatarsal II of Imperobator is unique among paravians for its parallelogram-shaped cross-section.
facts.quote: Metatarsal II is unique from that of other paravians in that it is parallelogram-shaped in cross-section

facts.statement: The incomplete claw of Imperobator features a prominent flexor heel, a trait also found in the paravian Balaur.
facts.quote: The incomplete ungual has a prominent flexor heel, a trait shared by the Romanian paravian Balaur

facts.statement: A 2025 study noted that Imperobator exhibits the sub-arctometatarsal condition seen in other unenlagiines like Austroraptor and Pamparaptor.
facts.quote: Motta and colleagues (2025) stated that Imperobator bears the sub-arctometatarsal condition observed in unenlagiines like Austroraptor, Pamparaptor, and others

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the size of Imperobator; while initially thought to be as large as Utahraptor, later revisions suggest it was smaller, comparable to Neuquenraptor and Deinonychus.
facts.quote: It was initially suggested that Imperobator may be one of the largest known paravians, comparable in size to gigantic dromaeosaurids such as Utahraptor and Austroraptor, but subsequent anatomical revisions suggested a body length similar to that of Neuquenraptor and Deinonychus

facts.statement: It is debated whether Imperobator is a dromaeosaur, as the fossil foot lacks the distinct sickle claw typical of that group.
facts.quote: The idea of the fossils being from a dromaeosaur is contentious, as the pes lacks the distinct sickle claw in addition to other characteristics of dromaeosaurs

facts.statement: A 2025 study raised doubts about the identification of certain leg bones, suggesting they might be fragments of metatarsals rather than the tibia and ankle bones originally described.
facts.quote: However, a 2025 study by Matías Motta and colleagues stated that the elements are too weathered to be sure that they represent the calcanea and tibiae. Instead, they could be incomplete condyle fragments from metatarsals

facts.statement: Before its official description, a 2007 paper assigned the specimen to the clade Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: a paper published in 2007 announced the specimen and assigned it to the clade Dromaeosauridae

facts.statement: The specimen lacked key dromaeosaurid traits, such as a prominent sickle claw, making that initial assignment problematic.
facts.quote: UCMP 276000 lacked multiple characteristics of dromaeosaurids, including a prominent sickle claw

facts.statement: The formal description assigned Imperobator to the clade Paraves.
facts.quote: The paper naming and describing Imperobator assigned it only to the clade Paraves

facts.statement: A 2019 analysis by Hartman et al. recovered Imperobator as a basal deinonychosaur outside the subgroups Dromaeosauridae, Unenlagiinae, and Troodontidae.
facts.quote: In a modified version of the large phylogenetic analysis of Theropoda by Hartman et al. (2019), Imperobator was recovered as a basal member of the Deinonychosauria outside of Dromaeosauridae, Unenlagiinae and Troodontidae

facts.statement: Researchers studying the unenlagiine Diuqin in 2024 considered Imperobator to be a possible member of that group.
facts.quote: In 2024, the describers of the unenlagiine Diuqin considered Imperobator as a possible unenlagiine

facts.statement: A 2025 re-analysis by Motta and colleagues consistently recovered Imperobator as a member of the Unenlagiinae.
facts.quote: A detailed re-analysis of Imperobator was published independently in 2025 by Motta and colleagues. In all variations of their phylogenetic analyses, Imperobator was recovered as a member of the Unenlagiinae

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Imperobator as Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Dromaeosauridae

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database classifies Imperobator within the family Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Dromaeosauridae

facts.statement: Imperobator lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Fossils of Imperobator are found only in the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation on James Ross Island, Antarctica.
facts.quote: Imperobator is known solely from the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation in James Ross Island, an island in the James Ross Island group on the northeastern edge of the Antarctic Peninsula

facts.statement: The habitat where Imperobator lived resembled modern high-latitude volcanic arches in terms of flora, climate, and environment.
facts.quote: The floral composition, habitat, and climate are of one similar to modern high latitude volcanic arches

facts.statement: During the Maastrichtian, the Antarctic Peninsula lacked large ice sheets due to a warmer and more humid global climate.
facts.quote: During the time in which Imperobator lived, Earth's climate was warmer and more humid than it is today and as a result the Antarctic Peninsula was without large ice sheets

facts.statement: The environment was dominated by Gondwanan subpolar forests containing both conifers and angiosperms.
facts.quote: The environment was dominated by Gondwanan subpolar conifer-angiosperm forests

facts.statement: Animals in this Antarctic environment still faced long periods of darkness and freezing winter temperatures similar to today.
facts.quote: The animals inhabiting Antarctica at this time would still have had to endure long periods of darkness and likely freezing temperatures during the winter, much like in modern-day Antarctica

facts.statement: Surface weathering on Imperobator fossils suggests they experienced minimal transport or reworking after death.
facts.quote: Imperobator fossils bear some surface weathering and abrasion, which indicate that they have gone through minimal transport, reworking, and sub-aerial weathering

facts.statement: Pollen from the Asteraceae family, found at the Imperobator site, represents the oldest known record of that plant group.
facts.quote: From the site in which Imperobator was found, pollen grains from Asteraceae, the group containing sunflowers and daisies, are the oldest records of the family that were collected

facts.statement: Evidence like peat mosses and clubmosses suggests parts of the environment were wet and bog-like.
facts.quote: Some of the environment may have been wet and similar to peat bogs, as evidenced by Sphagnaceae (peat mosses) and several other groups like the clubmoss Selaginella, the firmoss group Lycopodiaceae, and the clade Ericaceae

facts.statement: The formation yielded fossils of various animals including the ornithopod Morrosaurus, the bird Antarcticavis, the pterosaur Vegasaurus, mosasaurs, sharks, and bony fishes.
facts.quote: The Cape Lamb Member of the formation has yielded several other fossil remains, such as the herbivorous ornithopod Morrosaurus, an indeterminate hypsilophodontid ornithopod, the avian Antarcticavis, an indeterminate neornithine, an unnamed pterosaur, the elasmosaurid Vegasaurus; the mosasaurs Taniwhasaurus, Liodon, Plioplatecarpus, and Mosasaurus, sharks such as Notidanodon, and several bony fishes from the groups Teleostei, Actinopterygii, Ichthyodectiformes, and Sphenocephalidae

facts.statement: Shelled ammonites, aquatic cephalopods, are found in the layers of the Cape Lamb Member.
facts.quote: Shelled ammonites, a kind of aquatic, shelled cephalopod, are found in the layers of the Cape Lamb Member

facts.statement: It is debated whether Imperobator belongs to Dromaeosauridae or Unenlagiinae, with recent analyses supporting the latter.
facts.quote: In all variations of their phylogenetic analyses, Imperobator was recovered as a member of the Unenlagiinae. They identified new synapomorphies of the clade as well, such as the presence of a sub-arctometatarsalian metatarsus
